title: Question 8
stem:
Oxygen-15 ($^{15}_{8}\text{O}$) is radioactive and has a half-life of 2.04 minutes.

The decay of oxygen-15 produces positrons. For this reason, oxygen-15 is sometimes used as a tracer in positron emission tomography (PET scanning).

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by a tracer.

markscheme_points.text: substance absorbed by the tissues being studied

hints: Hint 1: Think about why doctors would want to put a radioactive source inside a patient - what do they want to follow or image?
Hint 2: Think of the two ideas needed for full credit - where the substance goes, and what it does once it is there in the organ under study.
parts.proper_answer: A tracer is a radioactive substance introduced into the body which is absorbed / taken up by the tissues being studied.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a Tracer Is For**
Imagine you want to see how blood flows or where oxygen is used in the brain. You cannot look inside directly, so you attach a tiny radioactive label to a substance the body already uses, like oxygen or glucose.

Step 2: **Putting the Definition Together**
So a tracer is first something you put into the body, and it must be radioactive so its radiation can be detected outside. Second, it must be taken up by the specific tissue or organ you want to study, so the detected signal maps that tissue. That gives both marking points.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: The equation for the decay of oxygen-15 is $$^{15}_{8}\text{O} \rightarrow ^{P}_{Q}\text{X} + ^{R}_{S}\beta^{+} + Z$$ where X is the nucleus formed during the decay and Z is another particle.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the values of the integers $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what must stay the same on both sides of any nuclear equation - total mass number on top and total charge on the bottom.
Hint 2: Recall what the top and bottom numbers are for a positron $\beta^+$ particle, then balance top numbers together and bottom numbers together.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Balance Nucleon Number on Top**
The top number is total nucleons. For the positron, $$R = 0$$ because a beta particle has essentially no mass. So $$15 = P + 0$$ giving $$P = 15$$.

Step 2: **Balance Proton Number - Charge on Bottom**
The bottom number is charge / proton number. A positron has charge $+1$, so $$S = +1$$. Then $$8 = Q + 1$$ giving $$Q = 7$$. This is nitrogen-15, as expected for $\beta^+$ decay where a proton changes to a neutron.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the name of particle Z.
hints: Hint 1: Think about $\beta^+$ decay at quark / lepton level - energy, momentum and lepton number must also be conserved, so a second very light particle must be emitted with the positron.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Missing Particle in Beta-Plus Decay**
In $\beta^+$ decay a proton becomes a neutron plus a positron. To conserve lepton number and energy-momentum, another lepton is needed. That is the (electron) neutrino, $\nu_e$. So $$Z$$ is the electron neutrino.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Define the activity of a sample.

markscheme_points.text: number of nuclear disintegrations per unit time

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is actually counted by a detector - it is not the number of atoms present, but how many of them break up in each second.
parts.proper_answer: Activity is the number of nuclear disintegrations per unit time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Meaning of Activity**
A sample contains many unstable nuclei $N$. Each second a certain number decay. Activity $A$ is that rate of decay: $$A = -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$$ In words, number of disintegrations per unit time, measured in $\text{Bq}$.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant of oxygen-15. Give a unit with your answer.
hints: Hint 1: Start from the link between how fast a sample decays and its half-life - a short half-life means a large probability of decay per second.
Hint 2: Check the time unit carefully - the half-life is given in minutes but the standard unit for the constant needs seconds, so convert first.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Half-Life to Decay Constant**
The decay constant $\lambda$ is the probability of decay per unit time. It is linked to half-life $T_{1/2}$ by $$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$$

Step 2: **Convert and Calculate**
Convert half-life to seconds: $$T_{1/2} = 2.04 \times 60 = 122.4 \text{ s}$$ Then $$\lambda = \frac{0.693}{122.4} = 5.66 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$$ The unit is $\text{s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Determine the rate at which positrons are produced in a sample of oxygen-15 that has a mass of $2.85 \times 10^{-6} \text{kg}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about how to turn a mass in kg into a count of atoms - you need the mass of one oxygen-15 atom.
Hint 2: Recall how to get the mass of one atom from its nucleon number using $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
Hint 3: Once you have the number of unstable nuclei $N$, think about how activity connects $N$ to the decay rate.
Hint 4: Remember each decay gives one positron, so the positron production rate equals the activity - now combine your steps numerically.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Number of Nuclei N**
Mass of one $^{15}\text{O}$ atom is about $15\text{ u}$: $$m_{atom} = 15 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$$ So number in $2.85 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$ is $$N = \frac{2.85 \times 10^{-6}}{15 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}}$$ $$N = 1.14 \times 10^{20}$$

Step 2: **Use Activity to Get Decay Rate**
Each disintegration produces one positron, so positron rate = activity $A$: $$A = \lambda N$$ Using $\lambda = 5.66 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$ from (c)(ii): $$A = 5.66 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.14 \times 10^{20}$$ $$A = 6.48 \times 10^{17} \text{ s}^{-1}$$

Step 3: **Interpret the Answer**
This huge rate reflects the very short half-life and large number of atoms even in a microgram sample. That is why oxygen-15 must be made on site for PET.

parts.label: (d)
parts.part_stem: The particles that are emitted from the body and detected outside it during PET scanning are not positrons but another type of particle.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.text: State the name of the particles that are detected.
hints: Hint 1: Think about which type of radiation can easily escape the body to reach detectors outside - positrons are charged and stop quickly, so what neutral highly penetrating radiation is used?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Escapes the Body**
Positrons travel only a few mm in tissue before stopping. What is actually detected outside in PET is the highly penetrating gamma photons produced after the positron stops.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: Explain how these particles are formed inside the body.

markscheme_points.text: annihilation results in their masses becoming photon energy

hints: Hint 1: Follow the positron after emission - it slows down in tissue and soon meets its antimatter opposite. What is that particle?
Hint 2: Think about what happens when matter meets antimatter - mass disappears and what form of energy appears to carry away $E = mc^2$?
parts.proper_answer: Emitted positron collides with an electron in the body and annihilation occurs, their mass being converted into photon energy (gamma photons).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Positron Meets Electron**
The $\beta^+$ particle slows by collisions and then meets an ordinary electron in tissue. Electron and positron are a particle-antiparticle pair.

Step 2: **Annihilation into Gamma Photons**
They annihilate each other. Total mass disappears and reappears as electromagnetic energy via $E = mc^2$, producing typically two gamma photons emitted back-to-back. These escape the body and are detected in coincidence by the PET scanner.
